name: ADS7828E_2K5
title: ADS7828: 12-bit, 8-channel, 50 kHz sampling A/D converter with I²C interface
summary: A 12-bit successive-approximation converter with an eight-input multiplexer, a built-in sample-and-hold, a self-timed conversion clock and a 2.5 V reference that can be switched on or bypassed for an external one. It runs from a single 2.7 V to 5 V supply and talks over a two-wire I²C bus in standard, fast and high-speed modes, reaching 50 kHz throughput at 3.4 MHz SCL. Inputs are used as eight single-ended channels against COM or four differential pairs, and two address pins let four of them share one bus. ADS7828E (±2 LSB INL max) and ADS7828EB (±1 LSB) come in TSSOP-16; ADS7828E/2K5 is the ±2 LSB grade on a 2500-piece reel.

circuits.title: Simplified I/O
circuits.description: The converter sits on a 2.7 V to 3.6 V rail shared with a microcontroller that is its I²C master. Its VDD pin is fed through a 5 Ω resistor and held up by a 1 µF to 10 µF capacitor at the pin, a second capacitor of the same range sitting on the rail itself. SDA and SCL each have a 2 kΩ pull-up to the rail. A0 and A1 both go to ground, setting both address select bits to 0. The reference pin carries 0.1 µF to ground, and all eight channels and COM come out as inputs.

equations.name: LSB size

where.VREF: reference voltage in use, internal or external

equations.note: 610 µV at VREF = 2.5 V; 1.22 mV at VREF = 5.0 V. Offset, gain and noise grow in LSB terms as VREF falls.

operation.text: A charge-redistribution SAR converter, so sampling is built into the capacitor array; made in a 0.6 µm CMOS process. An internal free-running oscillator times each conversion. Whenever the part is neither converting nor being addressed, the converter core is off and the oscillator stops.

On entering hold, the voltage at the chosen input is stored on the capacitor array. In the sample period the source has to charge about 25 pF; once charged, no more current flows. The average input current therefore depends on how fast conversions run.

Either the internal 2.5 V reference or an external one may be used. On a 5 V supply a 5 V external reference is needed for the input to span 0 V to VDD; on a 2.7 V supply the internal 2.5 V gives full range. An external reference may go as low as 50 mV. A smaller reference makes each code step smaller, so offset and gain errors look bigger when counted in LSBs.

With a 2.5 V reference, internal noise adds about 0.32 LSB peak-to-peak to the code. At a 50 mV reference it becomes 50 times bigger, about 16 LSB. The noise is Gaussian, so averaging successive results lowers it.

The part is always a slave and works in standard (100 kHz), fast (400 kHz) and high-speed (3.4 MHz) modes. SDA and SCL are open-drain. The master drives the clock and makes every START and STOP. Data on SDA must hold steady while SCL is high; a high-to-low SDA change with SCL high is START, low-to-high is STOP. Bytes are acknowledged on a ninth clock by the receiver pulling SDA low. When reading, the master leaves the last byte unacknowledged so the slave lets go of SDA and the master can send STOP.

The first byte after START holds the factory code 10010, then A1 and A0, then R/W (1 = read). The A1 and A0 pins are tied to VDD or digital ground and are latched at power-up, so up to four converters can share one bus. The part acknowledges when it sees its own code, select bits and R/W.
After a write address, the converter section powers up and starts converting once bit 4 of the command byte arrives. A valid command byte is acknowledged.

A conversion has to have been started before a result can be read. A read address is sent (address LSB = 1) and two bytes come back: four zeros then D11-D8, followed by D7-D0. Output coding is straight binary.

Sequence: START, write address, command byte, repeated START, read address, two data bytes (the master acknowledges the first and not the second), STOP. The converter stays powered down through the write address and the channel bits of the command byte, samples from PD1 to the acknowledge that ends the command byte, converts during the read address, then returns to whatever power-down state PD1-PD0 call for. Ending with a repeated START instead of STOP keeps the bus and is the quickest way to run back-to-back conversions.

The master first sends the HS master code 00001XXX in F/S mode, which goes unacknowledged; then, after a repeated START, the same write, command and read sequence follows at high speed. A conversion is not finished by the time the read address has been received, so the part holds SCL low after that byte until the result is ready. A STOP returns the bus to F/S mode; a repeated START keeps it in HS mode.

The internal reference is off at power-up. Every command byte must carry PD1 = 1 while the internal reference is in use; any command with PD1 = 0 turns it off. After it has been off, it turns on only once a command with PD1 = 1 has been followed by a STOP or repeated START, and the converter must then wait for it to settle before a 12-bit conversion: about 42 µs with no capacitor on REFIN/REFOUT and about 1240 µs with 1 µF. The usual way is a write address and a command byte with PD1 = 1, STOP, a wait for settling, then the normal read sequence. With an external reference, PD1 is 0 and the external source must already be settled.

The SAR core is upset by glitches on supply, reference, ground or digital inputs arriving just before the comparator latches; each of the n bit decisions is such a moment. Switching supplies, digital logic and high-power parts nearby are likely sources. Bypass VDD with 0.1 µF ceramic as close to the part as possible, plus 1 µF to 10 µF when the supply connection has high impedance. An external reference gets no rejection inside the part, so a reference tied to the supply passes its noise and ripple straight into the codes; 50 Hz or 60 Hz ripple is hard to filter out. Take GND to a clean, usually analog, ground away from the microcontroller's ground point; ideally the converter and its analog circuits get their own analog ground plane.
